acts.title: How a LAMMPS script is shaped

steps.title: Five sections, always in this order
steps.teach:
A LAMMPS input script is read strictly top to bottom, and the order matters: some commands only work *before* the simulation box exists, others only *after*. Rather than memorize that, we use five labelled sections and fill them in turn:

**1) Initialization** -- units, dimensionality, what an atom is
**2) System definition** -- the box and the atoms in it
**3) Settings** -- masses and how atoms interact
**4) Monitoring** -- what LAMMPS should report
**5) Run** -- what it should actually do

Your editor already holds this skeleton as comments. Everything after a `#` is a comment and is ignored.

steps.title: Anatomy of a dense command
steps.teach: Before writing anything, get used to reading. Click each token below to see what it does. This is the single most opaque line in the whole tutorial -- once it makes sense, the rest is easy.

steps.title: Work in reduced units
steps.teach:
Every number you type from here on needs a unit system. We want the one where the Lennard-Jones parameters are *defined* as 1 -- no angstroms, no kcal/mol, just dimensionless quantities. It is the usual choice when the point is general statistical mechanics rather than a specific material.

Write the command that selects it. The unit system is named after the potential.
hints: The command has the same name as the concept: it sets the units.
Two words. The second is the two-letter abbreviation for Lennard-Jones.
steps.reveal: `units lj` -- reduced units, where energies are in multiples of epsilon and distances in multiples of sigma.

feedback.correct: Reduced units. From now on a distance of 1.0 means one sigma, and an energy of 1.0 means one epsilon.
feedback.wrong: Not quite. This command takes exactly one argument: the name of the unit system.

steps.title: What if you just leave it out?
steps.teach: All four Initialization commands happen to match LAMMPS' own defaults. So what does omitting `boundary` actually do?

options.text: LAMMPS refuses to run without it
options.feedback: No. LAMMPS has a default for nearly every setting, and it will run happily without this line.

options.text: You silently get periodic boundaries in all three directions
options.feedback: Correct. `p p p` is the default. The reason to write it anyway is that the next person to read your script should not have to know the defaults -- and defaults can change between versions.
The opposite -- periodic is the default. Non-periodic is what you have to ask for explicitly, with `f`, `s`, or `m`.

steps.title: Close the box in every direction
steps.teach: Now write it explicitly anyway. Each of the three letters sets one direction -- x, y, then z. You want an atom leaving one face to re-enter through the opposite one, so the small box behaves like a slice of something much bigger.
hints: One letter per direction.
The letter stands for 'periodic'.
steps.reveal: `boundary p p p` -- periodic in x, y and z. The alternatives are `f` (fixed), `s` (shrink-wrapped) and `m` (shrink-wrapped with a minimum).

feedback.correct: Periodic in all three directions. The box now has no walls.
feedback.wrong: Each direction takes a single letter. You want the periodic one.

acts.title: System definition -- a box with atoms in it

steps.title: Mark out a region of space
steps.teach:
A *region* is a named shape in space. It is not the simulation box yet -- it is the geometry you will build the box from. Make it a cube running from -20 to 20 along each axis, so the box is 40 units on a side.

The six numbers are xlo xhi ylo yhi zlo zhi, in that order.
hints: Each axis needs a low bound and a high bound.
Every low bound is -20 and every high bound is 20.
steps.reveal: `region simbox block -20 20 -20 20 -20 20` -- a cube of side 40 centred on the origin, named `simbox`.

feedback.correct: A 40x40x40 cube named simbox. Nothing exists in it yet.
feedback.below: That bound is smaller than expected -- check which of the six numbers you are on.
feedback.above: That bound is larger than expected -- check which of the six numbers you are on.

steps.title: Turn the region into the simulation box
steps.teach:
Now build the actual box from that region, and tell LAMMPS up front that there will be **two** kinds of atom in it. That number is locked in from this moment: reference an atom type of 3 later and LAMMPS will stop with an error.

The command takes the number of atom types, then the region name.
hints: It creates the box. The name says so.
Three words: the command, how many atom types, and which region.
steps.reveal: `create_box 2 simbox` -- a box shaped like the `simbox` region, with space reserved for two atom types.

feedback.correct: The box exists and knows it will hold two atom types.
feedback.wrong: Two arguments: how many atom types, and the name of the region to build from.

steps.title: The region that wasn't there
steps.teach:
Here is a command that looks fine and is not. Read the error LAMMPS gives you -- the message names the problem precisely, and learning to read these is worth more than avoiding them.

Repair the line so it refers to the region you actually created.
hints: The error mentions a region. Compare the name here with the one you used two steps ago.
`simbo` is missing its last letter.
steps.reveal: `create_atoms 1 random 1500 34134 simbox overlap 0.3` -- the region is `simbox`, not `simbo`. LAMMPS looks region names up in a table and cannot guess at near-misses.

feedback.correct: 1500 atoms of type 1, dropped at random into the box, with `overlap 0.3` keeping them from landing on top of one another.
feedback.parse_error: LAMMPS resolves names exactly. A region ID that was never defined simply does not exist, so the lookup fails rather than guessing.

steps.title: Why bother with overlap 0.3?
steps.teach: Both `create_atoms` lines end with `overlap 0.3`, which refuses to place an atom within 0.3 length units of another. What goes wrong without it?

options.text: Nothing -- it only makes the packing tidier
options.feedback: It is not cosmetic. The Lennard-Jones repulsion goes as 1/r^12, so two atoms placed almost on top of each other carry an enormous energy and an enormous force.

options.text: Two atoms can land nearly on top of each other, producing a huge force
options.feedback: Exactly. That 1/r^12 term is unforgiving. The resulting force can throw an atom clear across the box in a single step -- which is precisely the failure you will cause deliberately in Act 6.

options.text: LAMMPS would place fewer atoms than requested
options.feedback: That is actually a risk *with* the constraint, not without it -- if the box is too crowded LAMMPS may fail to find room. Without the constraint it will happily place them overlapping.

steps.title: Add the second species
steps.teach:
Add 100 atoms of type **2**, again placed at random in `simbox` with the same overlap constraint, but using a different random seed -- 12756 -- so they are not placed in the same pattern as the first batch.

The arguments are: type, `random`, how many, the seed, the region, then `overlap 0.3`.
hints: Same shape as the line you just repaired, with type 2, 100 atoms, and seed 12756.
create_atoms 2 random 100 12756 ... then the region and the overlap constraint.
steps.reveal: `create_atoms 2 random 100 12756 simbox overlap 0.3` -- 100 atoms of the second type. A different seed gives a different random arrangement.

feedback.correct: 1600 atoms in total: 1500 small ones and 100 large ones. That is the binary mixture.
feedback.wrong: Compare argument by argument with the type 1 line: only the type, the count and the seed differ.

steps.title: Checkpoint -- you have a system
steps.teach:
The box exists and 1600 atoms are in it. LAMMPS still cannot compute anything, because no atom has a mass and no pair of atoms knows how to interact -- that is Act 3.

If you want to see what you have built, open the **Image Viewer** from the Run menu. Every atom is currently a point with no properties, but the geometry is real.

acts.title: Settings -- how atoms feel each other

steps.title: Give the heavy species its mass
steps.teach:
Every atom type needs a mass before LAMMPS will run. Type 1 is the light species with a mass of 1.0; type 2 is five times heavier.

Write the command that assigns a mass of 5.0 to atom type 2.
hints: The command is named after the property.
Three words: the command, the type, the value.
steps.reveal: `mass 2 5.0` -- atom type 2 weighs five reduced mass units. You also need `mass 1 1.0` for the light species.

feedback.correct: Type 2 is now five times heavier than type 1, so it will move more sluggishly at the same temperature.
feedback.wrong: Two arguments: which atom type, and what mass to give it.

steps.title: Reading the pair style
steps.teach:
`pair_style` is the single most important line in any LAMMPS script: it decides the physics. Click through each token to see what it carries.

The Lennard-Jones potential is `4*eps*[(sig/r)^12 - (sig/r)^6]`. The `12` term is the hard repulsion when atoms get too close; the `6` term is the weak long-range attraction that makes a fluid condense instead of dispersing.

steps.title: Choose where to stop computing
steps.teach:
The attractive term decays as `r^-6`, so beyond a few sigma the contribution is negligible -- but the cost of computing it is not. A *cutoff* truncates the interaction at a fixed distance.

Too short and you clip the attractive well entirely, and your fluid will not condense. Too long and you pay for forces that are essentially zero. This tutorial uses 4.0.
hints: Somewhere between two and six sigma is defensible. The tutorial picks one value in that range.
Drag the cutoff line on the plot until the well is comfortably inside it. The tutorial uses 4.0.
steps.reveal: `pair_style lj/cut 4.0`. A cutoff of 2.5 sigma is the more common convention in the literature; this tutorial uses 4.0, which keeps more of the attractive tail.

feedback.correct: Interactions are now computed out to that distance and ignored beyond it.
feedback.below: Too short. Below about 2 sigma you cut into the attractive well itself, and the fluid will not hold together.
feedback.above: That works, but you are paying compute for a force that is very close to zero out there.

steps.title: A pair_coeff that is missing something
steps.teach:
`pair_coeff` supplies the two Lennard-Jones parameters for a pair of atom types: **epsilon**, the depth of the well, and **sigma**, the distance where the energy crosses zero.

The line below gives only one number. Run it, read the real LAMMPS error, then repair it so type 1 interacts with type 1 using epsilon = 1.0 and sigma = 1.0.
hints: The error says the arguments are wrong. Count them: how many parameters does a Lennard-Jones pair need?
Two numbers after the two atom types: epsilon then sigma. Both are 1.0 here.
steps.reveal: `pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0` -- epsilon = 1.0 and sigma = 1.0. `lj/cut` needs both; there is no sensible default for either.

feedback.correct: Type 1 with type 1 is fully parameterized. You still need `pair_coeff 2 2 0.5 3.0` for the heavy species.
feedback.parse_error: LAMMPS counts the arguments a pair style needs and rejects the command outright when the count is wrong -- it will not invent a missing parameter.

steps.title: You never wrote pair_coeff 1 2
steps.teach: You have set the 1-1 interaction (eps 1.0, sigma 1.0) and the 2-2 interaction (eps 0.5, sigma 3.0). But a small atom will certainly meet a large one. What governs the 1-2 interaction?

options.text: LAMMPS errors out until you specify it
options.feedback: Not for this pair style. Some styles do demand every pair explicitly, but `lj/cut` fills in the gaps for you.

options.text: It is derived automatically as the geometric mean of the two
options.feedback: Right. By default eps_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 0.5) = 0.707 and sigma_12 = sqrt(1.0 x 3.0) = 1.732. The `pair_modify` command lets you choose a different mixing rule -- arithmetic mixing is the other common choice.
That would make the two species pass straight through each other. LAMMPS mixes the parameters instead.

steps.title: Checkpoint -- the system is parameterized
steps.teach:
Masses are set and every pair of types has parameters, whether you wrote them or LAMMPS mixed them. The system can now be evaluated: LAMMPS can compute a force on every atom and a total energy.

What it still lacks is any instruction about what to *do*.

acts.title: Monitoring and the first real run

steps.title: Ask for a report
steps.teach: LAMMPS prints a line of thermodynamic data every so many steps. Ask for one every 10 steps -- frequent, because the minimization you are about to run finishes quickly and you do not want to miss it.
hints: A small number, so output is frequent.
The tutorial uses 10.
steps.reveal: `thermo 10` -- one line of output every 10 steps.

feedback.correct: One report every few steps. Frequent enough to watch the energy fall.
feedback.below: That has to be a positive number of steps.
feedback.above: That is very infrequent -- this run is short, and you would see almost nothing.

steps.title: Where does the potential energy start?
steps.teach: You are about to compute the energy of 1600 atoms that were dropped into the box at *random* positions. Before you run it: will the initial potential energy be positive or negative?

options.text: Negative -- Lennard-Jones is an attractive potential
options.feedback: The well is negative, but that is not what dominates here. Random placement leaves some pairs much closer than sigma, and the 1/r^12 repulsion at short range is enormous and positive.

options.text: Positive -- random placement leaves atoms too close together
options.feedback: Correct, and this is the whole reason the next step is a minimization. `overlap 0.3` prevented the very worst contacts, but 0.3 is still well inside sigma for the heavy species, so plenty of pairs sit on the steep repulsive wall.

options.text: Almost exactly zero -- the attractions and repulsions cancel
options.feedback: There is no reason for them to cancel. The repulsive term diverges much faster than the attractive one, so close contacts dominate the sum.

steps.title: Relax the structure
steps.teach:
Rather than start dynamics from a bad configuration, first slide the atoms downhill into a nearby local minimum of the potential energy. LAMMPS does this iteratively, stopping when any one of four criteria is met: an energy tolerance, a force tolerance, a maximum number of iterations, and a maximum number of force evaluations -- in that order.

Use 1.0e-6 for both tolerances, 1000 iterations, and 10000 evaluations.
hints: One command, four numbers, in the order given above.
minimize <etol> <ftol> <maxiter> <maxeval>, so 1.0e-6 1.0e-6 1000 10000.
steps.reveal: `minimize 1.0e-6 1.0e-6 1000 10000`. Note that minimization finds a *local* minimum, not the global one -- for anything but a trivial system there is no way to reach the global minimum this way.

feedback.correct: Run it. Watch the potential energy fall from a large positive value to a negative one, quickly at first and then slowly as it plateaus.
feedback.wrong: Four numbers: two tolerances, then two iteration limits. Check the order.

steps.title: Checkpoint -- the atoms have settled
steps.teach:
The potential energy crossed from positive to negative. That sign change is the whole story: the atoms started jammed against each other and have moved to comfortable separations near the bottom of the LJ well.

Take a snapshot from the **Image Viewer** and compare it with the one from Act 2. The atoms are visibly clumping together.

During minimization there is no kinetic energy at all -- nothing is moving, atoms are simply relocated downhill. So the total energy equals the potential energy.

steps.title: Watch more quantities
steps.teach:
Once the atoms are moving there is more to watch: a temperature, a kinetic energy, and a potential energy that no longer equals the total. Ask LAMMPS for step, temperature, total energy, potential energy, kinetic energy, and pressure.

Fill in the two energy keywords that split the total: potential and kinetic.

editor.skeleton: thermo_style custom step temp etotal ___ ___ press

hints: Both are two-letter abbreviations.
Potential energy is `pe`; kinetic energy is `ke`. They satisfy pe + ke = etotal.
steps.reveal: `thermo_style custom step temp etotal pe ke press` -- and indeed U + K = E, which you can check column by column in the output.

feedback.correct: Now you can watch energy move between potential and kinetic while the total stays put.
feedback.wrong: Two-letter keywords. One for potential energy, one for kinetic energy.

steps.title: Integrate the equations of motion
steps.teach:
Nothing moves in LAMMPS unless a *fix* makes it move. You want the plain one: update every atom's position and velocity each step by integrating Newton's equations with the velocity-Verlet algorithm, adding no thermostat and no barostat.

Name the fix `mynve`, apply it to the group `all`, and use the integrator style whose name is the ensemble it produces.
hints: Every fix is: `fix <ID> <group> <style> ...`
The style is the three-letter ensemble: constant number, volume and energy.
steps.reveal: `fix mynve all nve` -- constant Number, Volume and Energy. With no thermostat and periodic boundaries, this is the microcanonical ensemble.

feedback.correct: The atoms will now actually move.
feedback.wrong: Four words: the command, an ID you choose, the group `all`, and the style.

steps.title: Choose a timestep
steps.teach:
The integrator advances time in discrete jumps. Each jump has to be short compared with the fastest motion in the system, or the algorithm will not track it. For Lennard-Jones in reduced units, 0.005 is a safe, conventional choice.

Remember this number. In the next act you are going to break it on purpose.

rules.label: the timestep, in reduced time units

hints: Small -- a few thousandths.
The tutorial uses 0.005.
steps.reveal: `timestep 0.005`. With 50000 steps that is 250 reduced time units of simulated time.

feedback.correct: Small enough that the integrator will track the fastest collisions faithfully.
feedback.below: That will work, but it is needlessly small -- you will spend a lot of compute simulating very little time.
feedback.above: Too large. That is heading for the instability you will meet in the next act -- try something smaller for now.

steps.title: Will the total energy stay constant?
steps.teach: NVE conserves total energy exactly, in exact arithmetic. You are about to run 50000 steps of it in floating point. What do you expect the total energy trace to look like?

options.text: Perfectly flat -- that is what NVE means
options.feedback: In exact arithmetic, yes. In practice the integrator has a finite timestep and floating-point rounding, so there is always some drift. A good NVE run keeps it small and non-systematic.

options.text: Small fluctuations around a constant value
options.feedback: Correct, and this is exactly what you should check in any NVE run. Energy sloshes between potential and kinetic while the total stays put. If the total starts climbing steadily, your timestep is too large -- which is the failure you will trigger next.

options.text: A steady rise, because the atoms are heating up
options.feedback: Not with a well-chosen timestep. Watch for it though -- a steadily rising total energy is the classic warning sign of an unstable integration, and you will see exactly that in the next act.

steps.title: Checkpoint -- run it
steps.teach:
Add `run 50000` and run the simulation.

The system starts far from equilibrium: potential energy falls while kinetic energy climbs, because the minimized structure has no thermal motion at all and the atoms accelerate down the potential gradients. After roughly 40000 steps both plateau and the system is equilibrated.

The temperature starts at 0 and settles near 1.5 -- nobody chose that value. It is whatever the potential energy released happens to produce.

steps.title: The most common failure in molecular dynamics
steps.teach:
Every MD practitioner meets this one, usually at the worst possible moment. It is far better to meet it here, in a system you can reset in ten seconds, than in a week-long production run.

You are going to raise the timestep by a factor of ten and watch the simulation destroy itself.

steps.title: Ten times the timestep
steps.teach:
Change `timestep 0.005` to `timestep 0.05` and re-run with a shorter run of 5000 steps.

Watch the total energy column. Report the total energy you see at the end of the run -- or, if the run dies before it finishes, report the last value you saw.
hints: Look at the `etotal` column in the Output window.
It will not be a small number. That is the point.
steps.reveal: The total energy climbs without bound. With a timestep this large, the integrator can step an atom straight through the repulsive core of its neighbour, and the atom comes out the other side with an enormous velocity.

feedback.correct: There it is. Energy is being created out of nothing -- the integrator is no longer solving the equations of motion, it is generating noise.
feedback.wrong: Check the `etotal` column in the Output window. Any large value is the right answer here.

steps.title: What 'lost atoms' actually means
steps.teach:
You may well have seen the run stop with **ERROR: Lost atoms**. Here is the mechanism:

The integrator moves each atom by velocity times timestep. If that jump is large enough, an atom lands *inside* a neighbour, where the 1/r^12 repulsion is astronomically large. The resulting force gives it a huge velocity, and on the next step it travels an enormous distance -- further than the neighbour-list machinery can account for. LAMMPS counts the atoms it can account for, finds fewer than it started with, and stops.

'Lost atoms' is almost never really about atoms being lost. It means your integration has gone unstable, and the timestep is the first thing to check.

steps.title: Put it back
steps.teach:
Repair the simulation. You know exactly what is wrong.

Note what LAMMPS did *not* do: it accepted `timestep 0.05` without a word of complaint, because that is perfectly valid syntax. No error message told you the value was wrong -- only the physics did. That is why watching the energy trace is not optional.
hints: The command is not malformed -- the *value* is wrong.
Go back to what you had before: 0.005.
steps.reveal: `timestep 0.005` -- back to a value the integrator can track.

feedback.correct: Stable again. You have now caused and repaired the single most common failure in molecular dynamics, in a system you could reset in ten seconds.
feedback.above: Still too large. That is the range that broke it -- go smaller.
feedback.below: That would be stable, but it is far smaller than necessary and wastes compute.

steps.title: Add a thermostat
steps.teach:
So far the temperature has been whatever the system happened to produce. To *choose* it, add a Langevin thermostat: the atoms get a friction term and a random kick, and the two balance at a target temperature.

The two numbers are the target temperature at the start and at the end of the run -- make them both 1.0 so the temperature is held constant rather than ramped. Then a damping time of 0.1 and a random seed.

rules.label: temperature at the start of the run
temperature at the end of the run

hints: Both numbers are the same, because you want a constant temperature.
Both are 1.0. Different values would produce a temperature ramp.
steps.reveal: `fix mylgv all langevin 1.0 1.0 0.1 10917` -- constant target temperature of 1.0. With a thermostat present the ensemble is canonical (NVT) rather than microcanonical.

feedback.correct: With `fix nve` and `fix langevin` together you are now sampling the canonical ensemble at T = 1.0. Shorten the run to 15000 steps and try it.
feedback.below: Both temperatures should be the same positive value.
feedback.above: Both temperatures should be the same value -- 1.0 here.

steps.title: Three things worth trying
steps.teach:
The script works. Now break it in more interesting ways -- nothing here is graded, and you can always reset.

**1. Change the mixture.** Swap the atom counts: 100 small and 1500 large. Does the heavy species still diffuse?

**2. Change the well depth.** Set `pair_coeff 2 2 2.0 3.0` so the heavy atoms attract each other strongly. Do they phase-separate?

**3. Ramp the temperature.** Give `fix langevin` different start and end temperatures -- say 1.0 and 3.0 -- and watch the system heat up over the run.

A reminder from the tutorial authors: every run here is deliberately short so it finishes on a laptop. None of it is long enough to produce statistically meaningful results.
